curation: Original English paraphrases of themes; no book text copied. Historical attribution strengths differ by record. These are heuristic cues, not position evaluations or engine calculations.

entries.author: Wilhelm Steinitz
entries.idea: Before advocating a direct king attack, establish a concrete reason that the opponent cannot defend adequately; lack of castling alone proves no win.
entries.goal: Identify the exploitable weakness and the opponent's strongest defense.

entries.author: Wilhelm Steinitz
entries.idea: Small positional assets can be developed methodically before seeking forcing play; a half-open file is a candidate asset, not proof of superiority.
entries.goal: Specify an entry square, target and the required supporting pieces.

entries.author: Wilhelm Steinitz
entries.idea: Material count and positional evaluation must be weighed separately; do not announce compensation or recovery without visible positional or calculated support.
entries.goal: Explain the actual imbalance and the confirmed practical resource, if any.

entries.author: Emanuel Lasker
entries.work: Lasker's Manual of Chess (1927), The Plan
entries.idea: Define a desirable resulting position first, then work backwards to the manoeuvres required; an isolated pawn calls for a concrete target arrangement, not a generic slogan.
entries.goal: State the desired piece placement and pawn structure, with risks.

entries.author: Emanuel Lasker
entries.work: Lasker's Manual of Chess (1927), The Combination
entries.idea: Check forcing sequences and defensive responses before following a slow positional plan; a geometrically attacked unprotected unit needs tactical verification.
entries.goal: Identify the attacked unit and whether the supplied variations actually resolve the threat.

entries.author: Emanuel Lasker
entries.work: Lasker's Manual of Chess (1927), Theory of the Openings
entries.idea: Ask which concrete arrangement would make undeveloped forces more effective and preserve king safety; castling status is only one clue.
entries.goal: Specify developmental priorities and which central operation becomes feasible.

entries.author: Aron Nimzowitsch
entries.idea: When confronting an enemy passed pawn, examine a stable blockading square and which piece can occupy it; do not claim an actual blockade unless the board supports it.
entries.goal: Name the pawn, possible blockade square, and a counter-resource.

entries.author: Aron Nimzowitsch
entries.idea: An established outpost may support long-term pressure and coordination; it is valuable only if its occupant has a useful role and cannot be neutralized cheaply.
entries.goal: Identify the occupant and a specific target or defensive task.

entries.author: Aron Nimzowitsch
entries.idea: Use a half-open file to examine rook penetration, coordination, and entry squares, without assuming the invasion is tactically possible.
entries.goal: Identify the file, possible entry square, and opposing counterplay.

entries.author: Aron Nimzowitsch
entries.idea: When an opponent occupies a weak complex, first consider how to restrict reinforcement or exchange the active piece before pursuing your own slow plan.
entries.goal: Identify the actual occupied weak square and the opponent's next useful move.

entries.author: Alexander Alekhine
entries.idea: In the style of Alekhine's annotated dynamic games, evaluate whether coordinated development can create a concrete central or king-side initiative; do not force an attack by analogy.
entries.goal: Describe the supporting pieces and the tactical reply that must be calculated.

entries.author: Alexander Alekhine
entries.idea: Illustrated by the precision of Alekhine's annotated games: turn a positional asset into a concrete next task, and calculate counterplay before calling the position winning.
entries.goal: Name the passed pawn and the required support, blockade-breaking or diversion.
